title: Prompt Like a Coach
goal: Your kid learns to get what they actually want from AI, by talking to it like a coach talks to a player: a clear picture first, clear words, then one change at a time. They make something real, like the pictures for a story they wrote, and learn when to start fresh, when to rest, and when good enough is good enough.
need: A grown-up's account on an AI image or chat tool
A real project that needs pictures or words, like a story
Paper to sketch or list what they want first
Patience, for you and for them

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: A few typed words and a hope rarely get the picture. Slow them down before the first prompt, help them name exactly what's wrong when it misses, and let them do the prompting.

plan.what: Picture it and describe it on paper (Steps 1 and 2).
Coach it one change at a time (Step 3).

plan.when: When it gets stuck, and at the end

troubleshoot.q: It keeps getting the same thing wrong
troubleshoot.a: Start a new conversation with a better first prompt. Old mistakes often carry over in the same chat.
Stop for the day. Coming back tomorrow with fresh eyes, and a fresh chat, often fixes it.

troubleshoot.q: They want to use photos of real people
troubleshoot.a: Keep real faces, names and photos of people out of AI tools. Describe characters instead.

lesson.text: AI follows what you say, not what you mean. A coach doesn't shout 'play better'. They say exactly what to change, one thing at a time. Prompts work the same way, and sometimes the best move is a fresh start, or a break.

model.line: The characters looking up, for a page of their book.
Looking left, the wrong details, an extra body part.
One change at a time, or a brand new conversation.
Some pages after a break until the next day, some with what it gave them.

lesson.modelNote: The pictures didn't get better from trying harder. They got better from smaller, clearer requests, fresh starts, and knowing when a picture was good enough for the book.

steps.title: Picture it first
steps.why: You can't describe what you haven't pictured. A clear idea first saves a lot of tries.
steps.kid: Before touching the screen, your kid sketches or lists what they want, using the Picture it card in the Prompt Coach Toolkit at the end of the guide: who's in it, what they're doing, where, and the style.
steps.you: Ask questions like a coach before the game: 'Where is she looking? Is it day or night? Cartoon or realistic?'
ask: What do you see in your head?
What's the one thing it has to get right?
steps.tip: Real projects work best, like pictures for a story they're writing. They'll care about every detail.

levels.explore: Draw a quick sketch of the picture you want, and say what's in it.
levels.develop: Fill in every part of the Picture it card before you start.
levels.extend: Plan a set of pictures for a whole story, with what must stay the same in each.

steps.title: Write the first prompt
steps.why: A clear first prompt does most of the work. Vague words get vague pictures.
steps.kid: Your kid turns the sketch into a prompt, using the Prompt parts card: who, doing what, where, the style, and what to show instead of what they don't want.
steps.you: Read it back to them out loud. If you can picture it from their words alone, it's ready.
ask: Could someone draw this from your words alone?
steps.tip: Directions are tricky. 'Looking up at the sky' works better than 'looking up'.

levels.explore: Say the prompt out loud while a parent types it.
levels.develop: Write a prompt with all five parts.
levels.extend: Write two different prompts for the same picture, and compare what each gets.

steps.title: Coach one change at a time
steps.why: Asking for five changes at once usually breaks the parts that were already right.
steps.kid: Your kid looks at the result, picks the most important thing to fix, and asks for only that, using the Coach talk card: 'Keep everything the same. Only change...'
steps.you: Help them name exactly what's wrong. 'It's bad' becomes 'she's looking left, she should look up'.
ask: What's the one thing to fix first?
What should stay exactly the same?
steps.tip: Name what to keep, not just what to change. AI needs to know what was already right.

levels.explore: Point at one thing to change, and say it in one sentence.
levels.develop: Fix three things, one at a time, and notice which ones worked.
levels.extend: Keep a list of the phrases that worked best, to reuse next time.

steps.title: Reset when it's stuck
steps.why: Sometimes the AI gets stuck on a mistake. Trying harder in the same chat rarely fixes it.
steps.kid: When it keeps getting it wrong, your kid picks a reset from the When it's stuck card: a new conversation, a rewritten prompt, a break until tomorrow, or keeping what it gave.
steps.you: Name the frustration, then choose the reset together. Stopping isn't failing.
ask: Is it getting closer, or stuck?
steps.tip: A new conversation with a better first prompt beats twenty fixes in an old one.

levels.explore: Start over with a parent, and say the prompt in a new way.
levels.develop: Use a new conversation, with a first prompt that includes what you learned.
levels.extend: Compare the stuck chat and the fresh one, and explain why the fresh one worked.

steps.title: Call it good enough
steps.why: The AI can keep making pictures forever. Your kid decides when one is good enough for the page.
steps.kid: Your kid picks the final pictures for their project, using the Good enough? card, and adds their own touches, like the words, the layout or a hand-drawn detail.
steps.you: Ask what they decided, not what the AI made. The choices are theirs.
ask: Is this good enough for your project?
What did you decide to keep, and why?
steps.tip: 'Good enough for the book' is a real skill. Perfect pictures aren't the goal; a finished project is.

levels.explore: Pick your favourite picture, and say why you chose it.
levels.develop: Choose the pictures for your project, and add your own words to each.
levels.extend: Before the next try, decide what 'good enough' means for this picture, then stop when you get there.

skills.name: Coaching
skills.text: one clear change at a time

conclusion.headline: They tell AI exactly what they want.
conclusion.text: Give them the next picture you need, a card or a poster, and say only what it's for. Let them run every prompt while you stay quiet.
conclusion.celebrate: When a hard picture finally comes out right, say: 'That took good coaching. You knew exactly what to ask for.'
extensions: Use the same coaching on a text answer, like a story idea or a recipe
Take a photo of a drawing you made, ask the AI to describe it, and see if its words would rebuild your picture
Draw one picture yourself for the project, next to the AI ones
Coach a person instead: describe a simple drawing to someone who can't see it, one instruction at a time, and compare

signs: They plan what they want before typing
They ask for one change at a time
They start fresh, or take a break, instead of fighting the tool
makeItReal: Pick a real project this month, like a story, a card or a poster, and let your kid coach the AI for its pictures, one change at a time.

fromHome.text: My two made a book together, with pictures they prompted themselves. Wrong details, extra body parts, a character looking left instead of up: it was really frustrating sometimes. One change at a time and a fresh conversation helped, and some days we stopped and came back tomorrow, or kept what it gave us.

classroom.intro: Coaching an AI works with a class when everyone plans on paper and you run the tool on the projector. Groups describe a picture for a real class project, then coach the AI one change at a time together.

tips.d: AI image and chat tools have age limits, so you type every prompt on your account at the front, following your school's device policy. Students write and read their prompts out loud.
Give the class something real to illustrate, like a class story, a poster for an event or a book the class wrote. Each group takes one picture from it.
In each group, one kid sketches with the Picture it card, one writes the prompt with the Prompt parts card, and one is the coach who names exactly what to change.
Groups take turns at the front. Each turn, the coach reads one Coach talk line, like 'Keep everything the same. Only change...', and the class watches what happens.
Explore students say one change in one sentence, Develop students fix three things one at a time, and Extend students plan a set of pictures that must stay the same across a story.
Keep real faces, names and photos of students out of every prompt. Describe characters instead. Finish with a share of what each group decided and which phrases worked best.

classroom.timing: Plan two or three sessions of about 40 minutes: Steps 1 and 2 on paper, then one or two sessions at the projector for Steps 3 to 5. Groups add their own words and drawings at school, and the finished project can go home.
